intro: Secure Authentication (SA) lets a DNP3 outstation, a field device such as an RTU, check that a command really comes from its master, the control room's SCADA system, and was not changed on the way. Before it carries out a critical request, such as opening a breaker, the outstation sends a challenge: a question that only a device holding the secret session key can answer. Nothing is encrypted: SA proves who sent a message, it does not hide it.
plain: DNP3 Secure Authentication adds a check to the commands a control room sends to distant equipment. Before it obeys an important command, such as switching off a power line, the equipment asks a fresh question, like a guard asking for a password. Only the real control room, which knows a shared secret, can answer it. A recorded answer played back later fails, because the question is new every time.

keys.title: Share session keys
keys.text: Before any command, SCADA gives the RTU (remote terminal unit) two new session keys: short-lived secret keys, one for each direction. It sends them wrapped (encrypted) with the update key, a long-term secret that both sides got beforehand. It repeats this regularly, so that no session key lives long.

operate.title: A critical command
operate.text: The operator opens breaker CB-1 so that a crew can work on the line. SCADA sends a direct operate: a command to act at once. The RTU treats it as critical and does not act yet. Only the application layer (the message itself) is shown here: the link and transport layers around it are the same as in the DNP3 lesson.

challenge.title: The RTU challenges
challenge.text: The RTU answers with a challenge: a new challenge number (CSQ 5) and 16 random bytes. Only the holder of the session key can answer it. The random bytes shown here are made up.

reply.title: Answer the challenge
reply.text: SCADA computes a MAC (message authentication code): a fingerprint of the challenge and its command that only the session key can produce. The method is HMAC, and SCADA sends the first 16 bytes of the result. The key itself never travels. The MAC shown here is made up: a real one depends on the key.

execute.title: Command carried out
execute.text: The RTU computes the same HMAC with its copy of the key. The two match, so it pulses the trip output (closes it briefly) and confirms. CB-1 opens.

replay.title: Replay attack blocked
replay.text: An attacker on the substation network recorded yesterday's close command and its reply. It sends both again: a replay attack. The RTU challenges with CSQ 6 and new random bytes, but the recorded reply answers CSQ 2, made with an old key. The RTU rejects it: CB-1 stays open and the crew stays safe.

frames.key-status-request: What is the state of your session keys?
frames.key-status: I have no session keys yet
frames.key-change: Here are two new session keys, wrapped
frames.key-ok: Keys set. Here is my proof
frames.response: Done: the trip pulse has started

notes.key-status-request: SCADA asks for the state of user 1's session keys: g120v4, in an AUTH_REQUEST (function 0x20). The bytes of the key exchange are not shown here.
notes.key-status: The RTU has no valid session keys yet: status NOT_INIT. Its answer, g120v5, also carries a key change number and fresh random data.
notes.key-change: SCADA makes two random session keys: one for what it sends, one for what the RTU sends. It wraps (encrypts) both with user 1's update key (AES key wrap) and sends them in g120v6.
notes.key-ok: The RTU unwraps the keys with its own copy of the update key. It answers with status OK and a MAC made with the new keys, which shows that it holds them.
notes.pulse: Not DNP3: the RTU closes its trip output for 1000 ms, the on time in the command, and CB-1 opens.

ac-3.name: App control
ac-3.note: 0xC3: FIR and FIN, a request in one fragment, sequence 3.

fc-direct-operate.name: Function 5
fc-direct-operate.note: DIRECT_OPERATE: act now, without a separate select (arming) request first.

g12v1.name: g12v1
g12v1.note: Group 12, variation 1: a control relay output block (CROB), one command for one output.

q17.name: Qualifier 0x17
q17.note: A 1-byte count, then a 1-byte index before each object.

index-0.name: Index 0
index-0.note: Output 0: the trip and close coils of CB-1.

trip.name: Control code
trip.note: 0x81: TRIP (open the breaker), as a pulse (PULSE_ON).

close.name: Control code
close.note: 0x41: CLOSE, as a pulse. It would put the line back under voltage, with the crew on it.

on-time.name: On time
on-time.note: 1000 ms, low byte first: how long the output stays closed.

off-time.name: Off time
off-time.note: 0 ms: there is no second pulse.

status-success.name: Status 0
status-success.note: SUCCESS: the RTU accepted the command and started the pulse.

ac-3-challenge.name: App control
ac-3-challenge.note: 0xC3: sequence 3, the same as the command it challenges.

fc-auth-response.name: Function 0x83
fc-auth-response.note: AUTH_RESPONSE: a Secure Authentication message from the outstation.

iin.name: IIN
iin.note: Internal indications, the outstation's status bits: no flags set.

size-24.name: Qualifier 0x5B
size-24.note: One object (01) whose size follows in 2 bytes: 0x0018 = 24 bytes.

csq-5.name: CSQ 5
csq-5.note: Challenge sequence number. It goes up with every challenge, so an old reply never fits a new one.

user-1.name: User 1
user-1.note: The user whose keys must answer. Each user has its own update key.

mal-4.name: MAC algorithm 4
mal-4.note: How the reply must be computed: HMAC-SHA-256, cut to 16 bytes.

rfc-1.name: Reason 1
rfc-1.note: CRITICAL: the request was critical, so it must be proven.

data-5.name: Challenge data
data-5.note: 16 random bytes, new for every challenge, shown in two parts. Made up here.

data-end.name: Challenge data
data-end.note: The last 8 of the 16 random bytes.

ac-3-reply.name: App control
ac-3-reply.note: 0xC3: still sequence 3. The command, the challenge, the reply and the response belong together.

fc-auth-request.name: Function 0x20
fc-auth-request.note: AUTH_REQUEST: a Secure Authentication message from the master.

mac-5.name: MAC
mac-5.note: The HMAC over the challenge and the command, with the session key, cut to 16 bytes and shown in two parts. Made up here: the real value depends on the secret key.

ac-3-response.name: App control
ac-3-response.note: 0xC3: sequence 3, the answer to the command.

fc-response.name: Function 0x81
fc-response.note: RESPONSE: the normal answer, sent only after the reply checked out.

ac-10.name: App control
ac-10.note: 0xCA: sequence 10. Every byte here is a copy of yesterday's message.

ac-10-challenge.name: App control
ac-10-challenge.note: 0xCA: sequence 10, the same as the command.

csq-6.name: CSQ 6
csq-6.note: A new challenge number. Nobody has answered challenge 6 yet.

data-6.name: Challenge data
data-6.note: New random bytes, shown in two parts. Made up here.

csq-2.name: CSQ 2
csq-2.note: Yesterday's challenge number. The RTU waits for an answer to 6.

mac-2.name: MAC
mac-2.note: Right for yesterday's challenge and key, wrong for today's. The RTU rejects the command. Made up here.

a-group.name: g120 · group 120
a-group.note: The group of DNP3 objects for Secure Authentication. A group says what kind of data it is: g1 is a binary input, g12 a command.

a-var.name: v1 · variation 1
a-var.note: The challenge: random data the outstation sends for the master to sign. v2 is the reply; v4 to v6 handle the session keys.

facts.transport: The DNP3 application layer: over TCP 20000, UDP or serial
facts.security: HMAC-SHA-256 with session keys. No encryption.
facts.frames: g120: challenge v1, reply v2, key status v4 and v5, key change v6

tips: SA proves who sent a message. It does not hide it: anyone on the line can still read commands and values. Add TLS encryption (IEC 62351-3) when that matters.
Aggressive mode saves a round trip: the master puts its MAC in the request itself (g120v3 and g120v9), based on the last challenge it got. Both sides must allow it.
Most failures at commissioning (the first start-up on site) come from a wrong update key or user number. The key change then fails, and the RTU rejects every critical request.
SA needs no clock: challenge numbers and random data, not time stamps, stop old messages from working again.

playground.file: The RTU's Secure Authentication settings. SCADA must use the same user number, MAC algorithm and key wrap, and hold the same update key.
playground.version: SAv5, from IEEE 1815-2012. Both sides must speak the same version.
playground.user: User 1. Each user has its own update key, so the RTU knows who sent a command.
playground.update-key: The update key is the long-term secret. It stays in the device's protected store and never travels unencrypted.
playground.key-wrap: How the session keys are wrapped (encrypted) in g120v6: AES-256 key wrap.
playground.mac: The MAC in each reply: HMAC-SHA-256, cut to 16 bytes.
playground.interval: The master changes the session keys every 15 minutes.
playground.timeout: How long the RTU waits for the reply to a challenge. After that, it drops the command.
playground.aggressive: Aggressive mode is off: every critical request is challenged.
playground.critical: The functions the RTU challenges. Reads are not in the list, so polling costs nothing extra.

anatomy.object: The name of the challenge object
